headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risk from shared filesystem/browser surfaces; no direct evidence of a dangerous default interaction.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx can observe Claude Code events and uses filesystem/MCP surfaces, while pdf.js processes PDF files in a browser-based worker model. If ctx ingests pdf.js outputs from a shared workspace or copied artifacts, malicious PDF content could be treated as instructions. The pairwise bridge is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF ctx reads pdf.js-generated files from a shared workspace without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF pdf.js output is manually copied into ctx prompts, attacker-controlled PDF text can steer ctx.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for ctx and pdf.js.
Require provenance labels on any file passed from pdf.js to ctx.
Disable automatic ingestion of PDF-derived text into prompts.
Review ctx hooks for any prompt construction from filesystem content.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing for PDF-derived artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and MCP servers, while pdf.js touches PDF documents and has no network egress. A shared filesystem or copied artifacts could move sensitive document content into ctx logs or graph data. Because pdf.js is local-only and the exact sharing path is undocumented, this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF PDF documents are placed in a shared directory that ctx indexes or logs, leakage can occur.
IF ctx records document-derived content into audit/runtime logs, sensitive PDF text may persist.
mitigations: Use separate directories with restrictive permissions.
Exclude PDF folders from ctx indexing.
Turn off verbose logging for document-processing runs.
Delete transient artifacts after each run.
requires-engineering: implement redaction before ctx writes logs or graph data.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support multiple instances and both write to filesystem-adjacent surfaces: ctx explicitly uses filesystem and MCP hooks, while pdf.js processes PDF files in browser-based tests. If they operate on the same directory or shared artifacts, concurrent writes or overwrites can corrupt outputs. The profiles do not show locking, so the conflict is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF both agents write into the same workspace directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF ctx hooks mutate files while pdf.js tests are running, race conditions can corrupt artifacts.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Run only one writer per workspace at a time.
Use read-only mounts for pdf.js inputs.
Add a quick preflight check for path collisions.
requires-engineering: add file-locking around shared mutable paths.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code events and can surface graph/runtime context, while pdf.js produces document-processing outputs. If ctx treats pdf.js output as authoritative and downstream automation consumes it without verification, errors in extracted PDF content can cascade into incorrect actions or records. The profiles do not document a verification step, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF ctx forwards pdf.js-derived text into downstream actions without validation, errors can propagate.
IF browser-based test output is used as ground truth by ctx, incorrect document parsing can cascade.
mitigations: Require human review before downstream action.
Compare extracted text against the source PDF for a sample page.
Mark pdf.js outputs as untrusted in ctx metadata.
Limit automation to read-only reporting.
requires-engineering: add verification gates before any action-taking step.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not show a residency or certification mismatch. ctx touches logs and graph data, while pdf.js touches PDF documents, but no PHI, EU-only, or retention-policy conflict is documented. Because the pairwise compliance pathway is not evidenced, this remains low and only if sensitive PDFs are introduced.
conditions: IF regulated PDF content is processed through ctx logs, retention policy review is needed.
IF a deployment adds jurisdiction-specific data handling not shown in the profiles, compliance risk may increase.
mitigations: Confirm retention settings for logs.
Avoid storing regulated PDFs in shared workspaces.
Document data-class handling for both agents.
Review jurisdictional requirements before deployment.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for regulated document flows.
